Field surveys of the Greater weever (Trachinus draco) in the Adriatic Sea have yielded detailed morphometric data for this benthic predator. The largest individuals recorded attain a maximum total length of 53 cm [Li = 53 cm], a size that places this species among the larger members of the Trachinidae family. Analysis of length-weight relationships indicates that the corresponding ultimate wet weight for a fish of this length reaches approximately 1020 grams [Wwi = approximately 1020 grams], a value derived from regional allometric equations. This substantial body mass reflects the species’ robust, laterally compressed body form, which facilitates its ambush hunting strategy within sandy and muddy substrates. The length-weight relationship also allows estimation of mass at earlier life stages; for instance, individuals at the onset of reproductive maturity, which occurs at a total length of 12 cm [Lp = 12 cm], are predicted to have a wet weight of roughly 11 grams [Wwp = roughly 11 grams]. These morphological benchmarks are critical for understanding the species’ life history strategy in the context of its coastal, temperate environment.

Field collections conducted during the peak spawning period at water temperatures averaging 10.9 °C [T = 10.9 °C] yielded a gonadosomatic index (GSI) of 8% [GSI = 8%]. The species exhibits a maximum lifespan of 10 years [am = 10 years] under typical environmental conditions, also recorded at 10.9 °C [T = 10.9 °C], which aligns with its temperate distribution and the observed trade-off between current reproductive output and future survival.

Early developmental parameters for the Greater weever have been characterized in controlled laboratory rearing experiments. Eggs incubated at a mean temperature of 16.8 °C [T = 16.8 °C] required an average of 4.5 days [ab = 4.5 days] to complete embryogenesis and undergo eclosion, a rapid developmental rate typical of temperate marine teleosts with pelagic larval stages. The newly hatched yolk-sac larva emerges from an egg with a diameter of approximately 1.04 mm, a dimension that constrains the initial mass of the offspring. Consequently, the wet weight at birth for these prolarvae is estimated at 0.000589 grams [Wwb = 0.000589 grams], a value derived directly from the egg volume assuming a spherical shape and standard yolk density. This minute mass underscores the extreme vulnerability of the early life stages, which must rapidly transition to exogenous feeding. The short incubation period at this temperature likely confers an advantage in variable coastal environments by reducing the window of egg vulnerability to benthic predators and physical disturbance.

The transition to reproductive maturity appears tightly linked to body size rather than age alone for Trachinus draco. Fish captured during trawl surveys begin to exhibit gonadal development upon reaching a total length of 12 cm [Lp = 12 cm], which corresponds to a body mass of 11 grams [Wwp = 11 grams] according to the established length-weight relationship. This size threshold for the onset of vitellogenesis and spermiation likely ensures that individuals have accumulated sufficient energy reserves to support the metabolic costs of gamete production. In contrast, the maximum recorded total length of 53 cm [Li = 53 cm] is achieved only by the oldest individuals, and the associated ultimate body mass of 1020 grams [Wwi = 1020 grams] represents the physiological ceiling for somatic growth under natural conditions. The considerable size range between puberty and the ultimate length — spanning over 40 cm — indicates a prolonged period of post-maturation growth, a pattern consistent with an iteroparous, indeterminate-growing teleost.

Comparative life history analysis places the Greater weever among temperate marine fishes with moderate longevity and a conservative reproductive strategy. The maximum lifespan of 10 years [am = 10 years] observed in field populations, recorded at a mean annual temperature of 10.9 °C [T = 10.9 °C], is intermediate between short-lived coastal species and longer-lived demersal predators in colder waters. The gonadosomatic index was 8% [GSI = 8%], assessed at 10.9 °C [T = 10.9 °C]. These values suggest that Trachinus draco maintains a balanced energy allocation between growth and reproduction, which may be an adaptation to the seasonally variable food availability in its shallow coastal habitat. The rapid development from egg to yolk-sac larva in 4.5 days [ab = 4.5 days] at 16.8 °C [T = 16.8 °C] is consistent with the need to exploit warm summer conditions for larval feeding, contributing to the species’ overall demographic resilience in a dynamic environment.
